newsitem.title: PERU: FEATURE - Ignoring hostage siege, Peru economy shines.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Ignoring hostage siege, Peru economy shines.

text.p: Unfettered by the international hostage crisis gripping the country, Peru's economy is quietly but firmly pushing ahead, ushering in a period of solid growth and subdued inflation.
"The economy in general is fairly robust, even more than was expected," said Guillermo Arbe, head of research at ING Barings. "Country risk is not a short-term concern."
Merrill Lynch's analyst Miguel Palomino agrees. "All major economic indicators have been pointing up in the past few months, and we expect them to continue doing so."

They and other analysts say the siege at the Japanese ambassador's residence where Marxist rebels have held 72 hostages since December 17 is a political blow to President Alberto Fujimori, but has had no effect on the economy.
"I haven't seen anyone drop their investment plans because of this," Pablo Secada of Santander Investment said a full four months into the crisis.

The fact is, investors have their eyes on Peru's fundamentals. And what they see are free market and privatisation policies that are pulling the country out of 1996's economic blues, crystallising into solid growth and lower inflation this year, and going forward.
Following three years of growth averaging nine percent, Peru's gross domestic product in 1996 rose 2.8 percent, as government steps to prevent overheating lingered longer than anticipated.
FUJIMORI SAYS ECONOMY BACK ON ITS FEET
But Fujimori recently told international central bankers that the economy was back on its feet and would grow about five percent in the near future.
Although that may be a bit optimistic, economists say four percent is likely and the direction is clear.

They see inflation at 10 percent or lower this year, with a clear downward bias. And they say the government's goal of 3-4 percent by 2000 is reasonable, provided no deviations from current policy occur.

Peru's stock exchange has historically attracted few foreign funds, but direct investment has averaged around $3.5 billion a year over the past four years, due mostly to the privatisation of the country's telecommunications and other state firms.

Although there is not much left to sell off, most contracts include long-term investment clauses which should help keep capital pouring in. By granting private firms concessions to carry out infrastructure projects, the government hopes to pocket an extra $8 billion.

Peru has also been able to slash its foreign debt by nearly 40 percent to $19 billion and roll over payments, bringing its debt burden to less agonizing levels. It clinched a deal last year with the Paris Club of creditor nations, and then a Brady pact with commercial banks on March 7.
Despite initial fears that hostage-related uncertainty could derail or at least delay Brady negotiations, they went along smoothly.
Even the country's $2 billion foreign trade deficit last year is largely written off by economists as part of the growing pains of an expanding economy.
PRAISE FOR WITHDRAWAL FROM ANDEAN GROUP

Fujimori's decision earlier this month to pull out of the Andean Group trade bloc after 28 years was saluted by the business community. Fujimori had told the Group, which links Venezuela, Colombia, Bolivia and Ecuador, to drop more barriers or lose Peru.

"Only Bolivia and Peru have followed World Trade Organisation parameters and adopted free economies with no subsidies or tariff restrictions," said Ricardo Guadalupe, Economic Studies manager with the National Exporters Association.
But for all the progress made, hard-bitten poverty has not yielded to healthier economic data.
First and foremost, analysts say, the economy is not generating enough well-paid jobs.

"All investments are being channelled to non-labour intensive areas such as mining, oil and public services companies, in particular electric utilities," said Secada. "So far these investments have deepened the unequal distribution of wealth in the country."
Palomino said economic growth should translate into more and better-paid jobs in the long run. But that can appear impossibly distant for nearly half of Peruvians, who live in poverty.
"That's the most important challenge the government is facing," Palomino said.
The scarcity of well-paid jobs also holds back consumption, a key component of any recovery. "Consumption is really depressed and no substantial recovery is expected during 1997," said Secada.
But the Achilles' heel of Peru's economic blossoming might ironically be "Fujimorization."
"All the advances, and all the reforms and all the stabilisation are linked to a single name -- Alberto Fujimori," said Arbe.

It is not clear if the president will attempt to overcome the legal hurdles that bar him from a third term. If he succeeds, it is even more unclear whether people would vote for him again in 1999 -- especially if he fails to put more money in their pockets.

There is consensus between Peruvian politicos and the man in the street that there is no going back on free-market reforms -- especially when that means hyperinflation, foreign debt default and the financial pandemonium experienced under former pesident Alan Garcia.
But, as Arbe put it:"The possibility that Fujimori might not win the election or might otherwise disappear from the political scene generates a fair amount of uncertainty."
